summary: Josh Albrecht, CTO of Imbue, presents Sculptor, an experimental coding agent environment designed to close the gap between prototype-quality AI-generated code and production-ready software. He argues that general improvements like larger context windows, speed, and output parsing will be solved by advancing models over 3-24 months, so builders should focus on domain-specific problems instead. Imbue's central problem is helping users trust AI-generated diffs—rather than manually reviewing every line or blindly merging, a secondary AI system can identify issues like race conditions or leaked API keys. He defines high-quality code as code with few defects, emphasizing synchronous, immediate feedback rather than late pull-request review. Four prevention strategies are detailed: (1) Learning—letting agents research existing technologies and solutions; (2) Planning—forcing agents to plan before coding via customizable system prompts; (3) Writing specs and docs as first-class workflow elements, with Sculptor detecting outdated documentation and highlighting conflicting specifications; (4) Enforcing strict style guides, including suggestions like making classes immutable to prevent race conditions. Three detection strategies follow. First, running linters (ruff, mypy, pylint) with automatic AI-driven fixes and before/after error tracking. Second, testing: LLMs can generate hundreds or thousands of potential inputs to find bugs via unhappy unit tests; generated tests can be discarded since regeneration is trivial; integration tests at the level of user meaning are where AI excels given clear test plans; test coverage combined with passing tests and LLM review provides enough confidence to merge; tests should run in sandboxes without secrets. Third, asking an LLM to review code for issues including spec violations, missing details, unimplemented specs, and custom best practices—with Sculptor enabling extensible checks. Albrecht notes that fixing issues is easier than expected, with simple strategies like trying multiple times in parallel enabled by robust sandboxing. He previews a future ecosystem of AI tools for debugging, logging, tracing, profiling, automated QA, visual design-to-code, and contextual search, and invites collaboration to integrate such tools into Sculptor.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Josh Albrecht introduces himself as CTO of Imbue, focused on robust AI software agents. He describes Sculptor as an experimental coding agent environment addressing the gap between vibe coding output and production-ready code, especially in larger established codebases.

sections.title: Focus on Domain-Specific Problems
sections.summary: Argues against building general improvements like larger context windows or faster parsing, since models will solve those in 3-24 months. Imbue focuses on helping users trust AI-generated diffs by having another AI system identify problems like race conditions or leaked API keys.

sections.title: Defining and Catching Problems Early
sections.summary: Defines high-quality code as code with few defects, citing academic software quality measurement. Emphasizes synchronous, immediate feedback over late pull-request review so problems are caught when easiest to fix.

sections.title: Four Prevention Strategies
sections.summary: Covers four prevention approaches: (1) Learning—researching existing solutions; (2) Planning—forcing agents to plan before coding via system prompt changes; (3) Writing specs and docs as first-class workflow elements with drift detection and conflict highlighting; (4) Strict style guides with suggestions like immutability for race condition prevention.

sections.title: Detection Strategy: Linters
sections.summary: Discusses running linters (ruff, mypy, pylint) with AI automatically fixing detected issues. Sculptor tracks errors before and after agent modifications to prevent introducing new errors even in imperfect codebases.

sections.title: Detection Strategy: Testing
sections.summary: Covers six testing insights: happy-path unit tests prove things work; unhappy unit tests via LLM-generated hundreds/thousands of inputs find bugs; generated tests can be discarded since regeneration is trivial; integration tests at the level of user meaning excel with AI and clear test plans; test coverage combined with passing tests and LLM review provides merge confidence; tests should run in sandboxes without secrets for safety and reliability.

sections.title: Detection Strategy: LLM Review
sections.summary: Describes LLM-based code review checking for issues before commit, spec violations, style guide and architecture rule violations, missing spec details, unimplemented or under-tested specs, and custom best practices. Sculptor enables users to extend checks with their own types of best practices.

sections.title: Fixing Issues
sections.summary: Notes that fixing issues is easier than finding them, citing 'a problem well stated is half solved.' Simple strategies like trying multiple times or running a hundred attempts with different agents in parallel work well, enabled by robust sandboxing that allows safe parallel execution subject to cost constraints.

sections.title: Future Tools and Conclusion
sections.summary: Previews a growing ecosystem of AI developer tools for debugging, logging, tracing, profiling, automated QA, visual design-to-code, and contextual search. Invites collaboration to integrate adjacent tools into Sculptor. Encourages attendees to try Sculptor at imbue.com and notes Imbue is hiring.

evidence.excerpt: I don't think that we really should be building any of these things. I think that what we really want to be building is things that are much more specific to the use case
evidence.supports: Builders should focus on domain-specific problems rather than general model improvements

evidence.excerpt: most of the things that I just mentioned are going to get solved over the next call it 3 to 12 to 24 months as models get better
evidence.supports: General improvements will be solved by advancing models within 3-24 months

evidence.excerpt: are there any race conditions? Did you leave your API key in there, etc. So we want to think about how do we help leverage AI tools not just to generate the code but to help us build trust in that code
evidence.supports: Core focus is building trust by identifying problems in AI-generated code

evidence.excerpt: sculptor does not work as like a pull request review tool because that's much much later in the process. Rather we want something that's synchronous and immediate
evidence.supports: Synchronous early feedback preferred over late PR review

evidence.excerpt: we try to encourage both the coding agents and our teammates to write things in a more functional immutable style to prevent certain classes of errors
evidence.supports: Style guide encourages functional immutable style to prevent errors

evidence.excerpt: the AI system understands what issues were there before it started and then what issues were there after it ran. So at least you can prevent the AI system from creating more errors
evidence.supports: Sculptor tracks before/after linter errors to prevent new errors

evidence.excerpt: you can have the LLM generate hundreds or even thousands of potential inputs, see what happens to those inputs, and then ask the LLM, does that look weird? And often when it says yes, that will be a bug
evidence.supports: LLM-generated fuzzing inputs find bugs through unhappy unit tests

evidence.excerpt: now that it's so easy to run LLM and generate the test suite again from scratch, there's a reason a good reason to not keep around too many unit tests of behavior you don't care about too much
evidence.supports: Disposable test suites are viable since AI can regenerate them trivially

evidence.excerpt: Integration tests are those that show you that your program actually works. Like from the user's perspective, like when the user clicks on this thing, does this other thing happen?
evidence.supports: Integration tests at the level of user meaning validate program behavior

evidence.excerpt: If I tell you so many lines have changed and also there's 100% test coverage and also all the tests pass and also a thing looked at the tests and thought they were reasonable. Now you can probably click on that merge button without quite as much fear
evidence.supports: Test coverage combined with passing tests and LLM review provides merge confidence

evidence.excerpt: A problem well stated is half solved. What this means is that if you really understand what went wrong, then it's much easier to solve the problem
evidence.supports: Fixing issues is easier than finding them once the problem is well understood

evidence.excerpt: even just try multiple times, try a hundred times with a different agent, it actually ends up like working out quite well. And one of the things that enables this is having really good sandboxing
evidence.supports: Parallel sandboxed retries are an effective simple strategy for fixing issues
